summary: Nyak Shul Khenpo Gyurmé Ösal studied under Shenphen Nangwa and Thubten Chökyi Dorje.

A Buddhist studies scholar, Nyanaponika Thera studied at the University of Ceylon, under Nyanatiloka Mahathera in 1937, and under Mahasi Sayadaw in ~1952. He founded the Buddhist Publication Society, serving as director and editor (1958–1984) and president (~1958–1988).

Specializing in Tibetology, Nyingcha Duoji studied at Boston University and completed a PhD at Harvard University (attested 2014) under doctoral supervisor Leonard W. J. van der Kuijp and teacher Mark Elliott.

Nyo Shul Lungtok Tenpé Gyaltsen studied under Patrul Rinpoche and Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo, and later taught figures including Khenpo Ngawang Pelzang, Thubten Chökyi Dorje, Terton Sogyal, and Jamyang Khyentse Chökyi Lodrö.

Nyoshul Khenpo Jamyang Dorje worked in Tibetology and Buddhist studies. He studied at Katok and Nyoshul monasteries and under traditional teachers Dudjom Jigdral Yeshe Dorje, Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche, and Rangjung Rigpe Dorje, later teaching numerous prominent students.
Nyoten Jimbo worked in Buddhist studies, having studied under Baisen Azegami. He held a professorship at Komazawa University.
Philosopher Octave Hamelin studied at Lycée Henri-IV. He taught at the University of Bordeaux (~1884–1905), École Normale Supérieure (~1903–1905), and the University of Paris (~1905–1907).

Active in Buddhist studies and Tibetology, Ogyen Trinley Dorje studied under Khenchen Thrangu Rinpoche (~2001), the 14th Dalai Lama (~2000), Drub Pön Dechen Rinpoche, Dragpa Tenpa Yarpel, Bokar Rinpoche, and Pema Donyo Nyinje.

Specializing in Iranian and Central Asian studies and linguistics, Olaf Hansen held posts at Humboldt University of Berlin (~1937–1944), the University of Jena (~1944–1945), and the Free University of Berlin (~1950–1968).

Olav Hackstein, a linguist in Iranian, Central Asian, and Indological studies, earned a Dr. phil. from the University of Freiburg (1983–1993). He held posts at Penn, Halle-Wittenberg, EPHE, and became full professor at the University of Munich in 2008.
Working in Buddhist studies, Indology, and philosophy, Ole Holten Pind completed his Dr. phil. at the University of Vienna by 2009 under doctoral supervisor Ernst Steinkellner.

Oleg Grabar worked in history, archaeology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. After degrees from the University of Paris, Harvard, and Princeton, he held posts at Michigan (1954–1969), Harvard (1969–1990), and the Institute for Advanced Study (1990–1998).

Oliver Codrington, working in history, archaeology, and Indology, served as Secretary of the Asiatic Society of Mumbai (attested 1878) and Honorary Librarian of the Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland (attested 1892).

Oliver Hector de Alwis Wijesekera worked in Indology and Buddhist studies. Educated at the University of Ceylon and SOAS, he was appointed Head of Sanskrit at Ceylon in 1943 and held visiting roles at Penn, Harvard, and Smith College.
Working in Indology, computational studies, and linguistics, Oliver Hellwig completed his habilitation under Harry Falk and holds an attested post at the University of Zurich (2024–2025).
Oliver Philipp Frey studied at the University of Vienna and held a post there, working in the fields of Indology and philosophy.

Olivier Lacombe worked in Indology and philosophy. He studied at the École Normale Supérieure (~1925–1928) and the Faculty of Arts of Paris, where he later taught (~1959–1970) before holding a post at Paris-Sorbonne University (~1970–1974).
In the field of Buddhist studies, Olivier de Bernon studied under Pierre L. Lamant and served as a professor at the University of California, Berkeley in ~2006.

A scholar of Indology and Buddhist studies, Olle Qvarnström studied at the University of Copenhagen, University of Washington, and Harvard University. He was supervised by Tord Olsson and served as responsible publisher at Lund University (attested 2000–2005).
Working in Indology and religious studies, Olli Littunen is attested in 2026 as a PhD candidate at Leiden University under the doctoral supervision of Peter C. Bisschop.
